Los Angeles Dodgers beat the Cincinnati Reds 8-2 on Thursday, September 17th, to clinch the National League West.
Kyle Tucker’s big day
Tucker has been fantastic lately, and Thursday’s game was a true cherry on top. He went 4-for-5 with two doubles, a home run, and a single, and drove in three runs.
Over the last seven games, Tucker has put up a .375/.467/.917 slash line with three home runs, nine RBIs, five walks, and three strikeouts.
Even over the last 15 games, Tucker is hitting .280/.383/.680 with five home runs and 11 RBIs.
Tucker nearly had a cycle, but when he gapped a ball in the eighth inning, he didn’t push for a triple and held up instead.
Still, this was Tucker’s game and a promising sign of things to come.
It was not just Tucker who played well, though; Freddie Freeman went 2-for-3 with an RBI and a walk, while Max Muncy went 2-for-4 with two RBIs.
Additionally, Miguel Rojas added the eighth run with a solo home run in the top of the ninth.
Considering the Dodgers went 0-for-11 with runners in scoring position on Wednesday, Thursday’s game was a welcome development.
Bullpen bounce-back
Justin Wrobleski looked great for three innings, allowing no hits and pitching them all perfect, with three strikeouts.
He was only at 32 pitches, and if Roberts wanted to stretch him out, he could have, but the Dodgers want to save his best stuff for the postseason.
Additionally, Landon Knack handled the bulk of the relief, allowing just four hits and recording two punchouts over four innings of clean work.
Blake Treinen and Seth Halvorsen each allowed a run, but thanks to Knack and Wrobleski, it was more than enough to finally clinch the division.

CINCINNATI — There is the road less traveled. And there is what the Dodgers do every year.
For the 13th time in the past 14 years, they are the National League West division champions. They clinched it with an 8-2 victory over the Cincinnati Reds Thursday afternoon.
The Dodgers scored seven times in the first four innings, leaving little doubt about the outcome.
There was little doubt about this year’s division title either.
The Dodgers spent a total of six days out of first place this season – two in April, four in May. They took over first place for good after beating the San Diego Padres on May 19. They had a double-digit lead for the first time on June 28 and have led by no less than seven games every day since.
Any drama is quickly draining from the playoff seeding race as well. Thursday’s win put the Dodgers four games up on the Atlanta Braves (off on Thursday) with a magic number of six to clinch one of the top two seeds and a first-round bye.
Clinching a postseason berth for the 14th consecutive season (tying the Braves’ MLB record) on Monday required only a champagne toast and a short speech from Dodgers manager Dave Roberts.
“This is kind of the expectation,” veteran Max Muncy said of that. “It’s not something you take for granted, but it’s the expectation that you can reach this point every single year.”
Clinching another division title, however, did not get the low-key treatment. The team celebrated in earnest.
No one had more reason to wash away the regular season and focus on the postseason than Kyle Tucker. The offseason’s big signing, Tucker has been a disappointment, making his four-year, $240 million contract stand out as the kind of mistake only the Dodgers could absorb.
But Tucker has shown signs of life recently.
He drove in the Dodgers’ first two runs Thursday with a first-inning home run, had an RBI double in the second inning, singled and scored a run in the fourth. With a shot at the cycle, he flew out in the fifth then doubled again in the eighth. Over his past eight games, Tucker is 12 for 29 (.414) with three doubles, a triple and four home runs.
Muncy had a two-run double in the fourth inning and Freddie Freeman went 2 for 3 with two runs scored and a sacrifice fly. Miguel Rojas hit a solo home run in the ninth.
The early lead made the bullpen game a smooth ride. Justin Wrobleski started and retired all nine batters he faced. Blake Treinen gave up a solo home run to Sal Stewart in the fourth inning. But Landon Knack followed that with four scoreless innings.

They hit their magic number, but minus the magic.
The Dodgers trudged toward October by clinching their 13th National League West title in 14 years on Thursday, their customary march mired in a quicksand of questions.
Has any Dodger team during this golden era entered the playoffs with more injuries, more uncertainty, and a greater fear of underachievement?
Will the party in Cincinnati be the last time they celebrate this season?
The magic is indeed missing, and after two seasons of conjuring up postseason greatness, these back-to-reality Dodgers appear headed for an early fall.
The Three-Peat looks like a no-go.
Despite the best efforts from baseball’s best braintrust, their latest creation simply doesn’t have the appearance of a championship team.
They’re aging, they’re hurting and, with only a couple of weeks left until the beginning of their annual autumnal angst, they look tired and taut and unprepared for this monumental tussle with history.
“I think for me, the message was, ‘We haven’t come close to playing our best baseball yet.’” manager Dave Roberts told reporters when relaying his speech to the team earlier this week upon clinching a record-tying 14th consecutive playoff berth.
He added, “The message was, we’ve accomplished a lot up to this point, all the while not playing our best baseball. So let’s get some of these guys healthy.”
Haven’t come close to playing our best baseball… Let’s get some of these guys healthy.
Not exactly “Win one for the Gipper” stuff, but completely accurate. These postseason’s themes are more realistic than inspirational, and for good reason.
No, they haven’t come close to playing their best baseball. Forget what you see in these season-ending games against some of the worst teams. Remember, instead, what they’ve done against some of baseball’s best.
Since the All-Star break, they are 4-12 against the five National League playoff contenders. The Atlanta Braves swept them. The Chicago Cubs swept them. The Milwaukee Brewers dominated them.
These teams will be waiting for them in October, and even baseball’s richest roster might not be enough to carry this staggered bunch through their toughest stretch. They’ve played a lot of games in three years, all under baseball’s brightest spotlight, every night, scores of media, millions of fans, a worldwide whirl for 28 regular dudes, and it’s finally taken its toll.
They’ve hit the wall… and the wall is about to hit back.
“It’s not easy, I think it’s a lot harder than people think it is,” said Roberts. “Human nature alone, when you’re hungry, when you’re chasing something, it’s a lot more easy to be motivated, versus, having been there, done that, it gets a little trite, a little old.”
He added: “To keep guys enthusiastic, focused, hungry, that’s harder. But to their credit, they stayed the course. And for me, we’re just as hungry as we were in ‘24 and ‘25. This is a separate season. Our guys understand.”
The 1988-89 Lakers understood, too. And they still got burned in ways that Dodger fans will find painfully familiar. Showtime was chasing the original “three-peat” trademarked by Pat Riley when the Lakers were swept by the Detroit Pistons in a Finals that seemed cursed,
Byron Scott missed the series with a hamstring injury and Magic Johnson essentially missed the final two games with a hamstring injury and they couldn’t survive.
This looks like the Dodgers today. Their injuries feel too major, and the impact too deep.
Start with Shohei Ohtani. The Dodgers haven’t won a full-season championship in 38 years without him at the top of the lineup. He’ll be there again, but his body has been breaking down for the last couple of months, and, before being recently placed on the injured list — finally! — he was only a shadow of himself.
He hasn’t hit a home run or driven in a run outside of Coors Field in more than a month. In his last 24 games before going on the IL with biceps and knee issues, he was batting .198. The Dodgers can’t admit it, and Ohtani would never acknowledge it, but this is a man in serious need of an extended rest.
Teoscar Hernández’s two-run homer Tuesday in the Dodgers’ win against the Reds was his second home run in as many nights.
Also on the injured list in these final days is Andy Pages, who was having a career year before breaking his hand. He’ll return without much time to get ready for October, and this is a man who will need some time, as he has a career .114 average in the postseason and was even benched last year before he redeemed himself with that picturesque catch over Kiké Hernández.
Speaking of last October’s heroes, the biggest savior has also spent the summer in pain, Will Smith battling neck issues until recently returning to the lineup. But the comeback has been bumpy. In his initial games since returning at the start of September, Smith was batting .171. Last October he set a major league record by catching 73 innings in the World Series. He is still paying the price.
Then there’s Freddie Freeman, whose bat doesn’t have the same pop, who’s step doesn’t have the same spring, and who has his worst OPS in 14 years. Add an inconsistent Mookie Betts and an incredibly streaky Teoscar Hernández to an already-shaky lineup.
It’s been such an unsteady year, Andrew Friedman’s two big offseason acquisitions have been busts. Edwin Díaz has been terrible, and then injured, then terrible again. Kyle Tucker has been terrible, then worse, then mostly invisible.
Even the Dodgers two role-playing heroes have seemingly disappeared. Kiké Hernández, at age 35, has his lowest home-run total — three — in 12 years. Miguel Rojas, at age 37, has his lowest home run and RBI totals in nine years.
The Dodgers clinch a playoff berth with their 4-1 victory over the Cincinnati Reds, reaching the postseason for a record-tying 14th consecutive year.
As if they didn’t have enough problems on the field and at the plate, check out the mound. No, don’t.
Even what should be their strength is now being threatened. Blake Snell left Wednesday’s game early with groin issues and Tyler Glasnow recently complained of general discomfort. This leaves a proven playoff rotation of two, Yoshinobu Yamamoto and Tarik Skubal, and if you think Yamamoto threw a lot of innings last October, this time he won’t be able to leave the mound for a month.
In all, this is a Dodger team facing its toughest challenge yet, their quest for an historic three-peat much tougher than the last two journeys, one that will require arguably the greatest stretch of baseball in franchise history to complete.
This division title is a nice beginning.
It could also be the end.

The Los Angeles Dodgers brought third baseman Max Muncy and outfielder Josue De Paula back into the lineup for Thursday’s series finale against the Cincinnati Reds.
The Dodgers lost Wednesday’s game after Cy Young winner Blake Snell went down with a groin injury after pitching just one inning. Luckily, Snell believes he can still make a start before the end of the regular season, which ends in less than two weeks.
LA won the first two games of the series, shutting down a powerful Reds lineup, and will look to do the same to win the series Wednesday.
Who is Starting for the Dodgers?
Justin Wrobleski will start for the Dodgers on Wednesday, making his 25th appearance of the regular season. Two of his last three appearances have come out of the bullpen, and none of them have lasted more than three innings since his return from the injured list with a forearm problem.
He has a 3.78 ERA on the year, striking out 111 batters over the course of 133.1 innings—his heaviest workload in an MLB season so far.
How deep into the game he goes depends on him, but the Dodgers will have backup in the form of Landon Knack whenever Wrobleski is ready to come out.
Who is in the Dodgers’ Lineup?
The Dodgers still don’t have Shohei Ohtani in the lineup, but Tommy Edman has replaced him well and will play center field on Thursday. Freddie Freeman moves up a couple of spots into the No. 2 hole, followed by right fielder Kyle Tucker, who will bat third.
Left fielder Teoscar Hernandez takes over the cleanup spot, followed by Muncy, who slides back into third base and bats fifth. De Paula serves as the designated hitter and will bat sixth, with catcher Hunter Feduccia giving Will Smith an off day in the No. 7 spot.
Second baseman Alex Freeland will bat eight for the Dodgers, with Miguel Rojas rounding out the lineup and playing shortstop—giving Mookie Betts a well-deserved rest day.

Who is Starting for the Reds?
Veteran right-hander Brady Singer is starting for the Reds, making his 30th appearance of the season. He has reached that mark in each of the last three seasons, and has 25 or more appearances in all seven of his MLB campaigns bar 2020.
He isn’t having the best year despite his regular consistency, though, as he has a 5.38 ERA through 150.2 innings with only 125 strikeouts on the season.
Singer didn’t face the Dodgers in last week’s series in Los Angeles, but he has a pretty good track record against the team. In three appearances against LA, all of which came during his time with Kansas City, he has a 1.89 ERA through 19 innings with 15 strikeouts.
The Dodgers will hope to break that trend on Thursday as they look to bring themselves even closer to a first-round postseason bye. The first pitch of Thursday’s game comes at 9:40 p.m. PT.

The Los Angeles Dodgers have a difficult decision ahead as they prepare for the postseason, and it could mean a harsh end for a star offseason acquisition.
With All-Star reliever Edwin Diaz struggling to earn his way back into the bullpen following an injury, the team has indicated that he won't be guaranteed a spot on the playoff roster.
"All-Star closer Edwin Díaz continues to struggle, as Tanner Scott did a year ago, and his rehab assignment with Triple-A Oklahoma City has gone poorly enough that Dodgers manager Dave Roberts acknowledged Monday the club could leave the three-time All-Star closer off the postseason roster," Fabian Ardaya wrote for The Athletic.
That uncertainty creates an obvious question about another high-profile Dodgers addition who has struggled throughout his first season in Los Angeles: Kyle Tucker.
The four-time All-Star signed a four-year, $240 million contract with the Dodgers during the offseason, but his production has fallen well short of what the team presumably expected when it made that investment.
Los Angeles Dodgers Send Definitive Kyle Tucker Message With Playoffs Looming
Though the Dodgers' willingness to leave Diaz off of the postseason roster suggests the team is evaluating performance alone, Roberts sent a clear message about any upcoming roster decisions involving Tucker.
"I told him, I'm gonna ride or die with him," Roberts said, according to the New York Post's Jack Harris.
That commitment comes despite a season in which Tucker has produced a .226/.327/.374 slash line with 15 home runs and 66 RBI through 143 games, soliciting calls that he be benched or platooned, if not removed from the upcoming playoff roster altogether. His performance has also been dramatically different at home than it has been on the road. Tucker has hit .187 with a .572 OPS at Dodger Stadium, compared with a .266 average and .826 OPS away from home.
That split adds another layer to the pressure surrounding Tucker as the Dodgers move toward the postseason.
$240 Million Los Angeles Dodgers Disappointment Brings Kyle Tucker Playoff Question Into Focus
Roberts' definitive commitment is particularly notable given how disappointing his first season has been relative to his contract.
"At this point, it is all adding up to a lost season for the 29-year-old, who is threatening to become one of the biggest free-agent flops in at least the sport's recent high-priced history," Harris added. "And yet, the Dodgers aren't wavering from their commitment to keep playing the four-time All-Star, rolling the dice 'talent level' and 'proven track record,' as Roberts cited, by keeping him in the lineup for the long haul."
That gives Tucker a clear path to remain part of the Dodgers' postseason plans, even as the club evaluates other difficult roster decisions.
This article was originally published on Forbes.com

Los Angeles Dodgers star Kyle Tucker may be getting hot just in time for the playoffs.
The National League West-leading Dodgers (90-57) will look to extend their winning streak to nine games when they visit the Miami Marlins (72-76) on Saturday. The Marlins, in turn, have lost seven of their past eight games.
Tucker went 3-for-3 with a season-high five RBIs in Los Angeles’ 6-2 victory over Miami on Friday. He fell a double short of the cycle.
Entering Friday, Tucker was on pace for his fourth straight month with an OPS at or below .700, and that’s not what the Dodgers thought they were getting when they signed him to a four-year, $240 million contract in January.
Tucker, who has posted OPS numbers of .993 and .841 over the past two years, impressed Marlins manager Clayton McCullough with his performance on Friday.
“Independent of how this season has gone, (Tucker) is still a terrific hitter,” McCullough said. “He handles lefties well. He got a hanging breaking ball and turned the game for them.”
Tucker produced five straight seasons with more than 20 homers before mustering just 14 in 2026. But if he can finish strong, that will help a Dodgers squad that is missing injured sluggers Shohei Ohtani (right biceps inflammation), Freddie Freeman (right knee) and Andy Pages (left hand). Those three players have hit a combined 67 homers this season.
Los Angeles also saw Josue De Paula make his MLB debut on Friday. De Paula went 0-for-3 with a walk after tearing up Double-A pitching.
“We want to get him some major-league at-bats to see what it looks like,” Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said.
The Dodgers will turn to right-hander Tyler Glasnow (4-0, 3.12 ERA) to make the start on Saturday.
His per-nine-innings averages are outstanding in terms of hits allowed (5.3), walks (2.7) and strikeouts (10.9). The Dodgers are 8-2 when he starts, and this will be his fourth start since coming back from a near-three-month injury absence.
Glasnow is 1-1 with a 3.86 ERA in five career starts versus the Marlins.
Miami will counter with right-hander Tyler Phillips (5-6, 3.51), who is 1-0 with a 6.94 ERA in six career appearances (one start) against the Dodgers.
For his career overall, Phillips has a sterling 2.49 ERA in 71 relief appearances, but a 5.13 ERA in 25 career starts.
As for Miami’s offense, the Marlins are hoping that shortstop Otto Lopez is back on track after a 4-for-5 performance on Friday.
This year, Lopez hit .322 in March/April; .339 in May; and .340 in June. That hot start made him a first-time All-Star. However, he batted .284 in July and just .236 in August.
Thanks to Friday’s big game, he is now hitting .342 in September.
“After the phenomenal first half, he struggled for a bit,” McCullough said. “He looks to be back in a good spot, hitting the ball to all fields. It’s something we have grown accustomed to, and it bodes well for us to have him get hits in bunches.”
–Field Level Media

Teoscar Hernández Is Delivering When The Dodgers Need Him The Most
LOS ANGELES — During a months-long spiral at the plate, Teoscar Hernández tried to maintain his upbeat, convivial persona.
But for much of the summer, before his September revival, it was difficult for the Dodgers’ fun-loving, seed-tossing veteran presence to look or feel like himself.
"I try to stay positive and bring the same energy that you guys know and see everyday — smiling, making jokes," Hernández told me. "But at the same time, it’s really hard."
(Photo by David Jordan/MLB Photos via Getty Images)
Dodgers manager Dave Roberts noticed his typically jovial outfielder looking a bit more sullen at times, too. It was understandable.
Hernández, a fixture in the Dodgers’ lineup whose clutch hitting, encouraging nature and penchant for performing on the sport’s biggest stage helped his team win back-to-back World Series titles, had a respectable .785 OPS when he went on the injured list on May 29 with a left hamstring strain.
But the 33-year-old did not look the same when he returned a month later. From June 29 to Aug. 29, his .592 OPS was the ninth-lowest mark among all qualified MLB hitters over that stretch.
"Some of the joy was sucked out," Roberts told me, "because it’s hard to be so joyful when you’re not performing. He was still a good teammate, always a good teammate, but I know there were a lot of frustrating moments for him."
Hernández’s struggles were compounded by the fact that the Dodgers were also getting little from their other corner outfielder, Kyle Tucker, or the rest of an offense that looked lifeless for much of the summer.
But now, at a crucial juncture for his team with All-Stars Shohei Ohtani and Andy Pages sidelined, another All-Star in Freddie Freeman battling knee soreness and the playoffs just weeks away, Hernández is taking his frustration out constructively.
He is annihilating the baseball in September, leaving his summer slump behind and giving the Dodgers reason to believe in the depth of their offense again.
"When he catches fire," Dodgers infielder Tommy Edman said, "he’s as good as anybody in the game."
Even among Hernández’s best career stretches, the tear he’s on now stands out. Every part of his offensive profile is enhanced.
Hernández, who’s prone to swing and miss even when he’s going right, is making better swing decisions. From last month to this month, he has lowered his chase rate from 36.7% to 24.8%, tripled his walk rate from 4.3% to 15.1% and cut his strikeout rate nearly in half from 31.2% to 18.9%.
And along with a more selective approach, he is punishing every mistake in a way he couldn’t earlier this season.
Hernández’s hard-hit rate has skyrocketed from 34.5% in July to 47.5% in August to 60% this month. His average exit velocity this September (96.6 mph) is the highest of any month in his career.
Eight of his 10 hardest-hit balls this season have come in the last two weeks, and his power is being generated by the highest average bat speed he has produced in any month over the last two seasons (74.1 mph).
It’s a far cry from where Hernández was just a couple of weeks ago, when his year-long struggle against right-handers had the Dodgers considering using a platoon in left field. That no longer appears to be a consideration.
"Right now," Roberts said, "it’s just night and day."
So how, exactly, did Hernández find his way back?
"The most important part, he’s healthy," Dodgers infielder Miguel Rojas told me. "If he’s healthy, we can see the Teo that’s running hard on the bases, stealing bases, going first to third. Obviously the bat is there because it’s his best tool, but seeing the complete player now is really refreshing."
Earlier this season, Hernández’s downturn looked familiar.
A year ago, he had the highest batting average on the team when he went on the IL in May with an adductor strain. He returned two weeks later, then watched his OPS precipitously drop 200 points from May 21 (.927) to July 21 (.727).
Clearly, the lower-body injury had lingered, throwing off his swing and sapping his power.
This year, it was happening again, only with his hamstring. The swing that worked for him before the injury was putting too much pressure on his lower half. Upon his return from the IL, he had a .562 OPS overall in July and a team-worst .496 OPS against right-handed pitching in August.
"I told Dave, ‘If you feel like you have to use somebody else in there, just do it,’" Hernández said.
(Photo by Meg Oliphant/Getty Images)
That would not be necessary. At least, not again after Aug. 25. The decision to sit him that day was noteworthy, considering the Dodgers were coming off an off day and facing a Braves team they were battling for a first-round bye.
In hindsight, it might have served as a wake-up call.
On Aug. 26, Hernández returned to the lineup in Atlanta with a two-hit day. He then ended the Dodgers’ next series in Detroit with a two-run homer off Framber Valdez, which might have been the turning point.
"I think that at-bat gave him the extra life that he needed for the last part of the season," Rojas said. "Obviously, baseball is about confidence, and you find confidence with success, and I thought that’s what he needed. He needed, like, one good swing that he knows he’s back, and then all of a sudden we see the results we get now."
There’s also a mechanical component to Hernández’s upswing.
Too often, Hernández felt both rushed and late at the plate as he worked his way back from his hamstring injury. He has since opened his stance in an effort, he says, to slow his body up, prevent his front hip from flying open and give him more time to see the ball. He has also traded his more subtle toe tap for a slightly more exaggerated leg lift and hip twist as a timing mechanism that seems to be producing more power.
These were moves he used before in his career. Now healthy, he feels his body can withstand the added force once again.
Sometimes with hitting, the littlest tweaks can yield the biggest results.
"That’s why it’s hard," Hernández told me. "One day, you don’t know what you’re doing. The next day, you change barely — sometimes it’s your hands, sometimes it’s your legs, sometimes it’s how low, how tall [in the stance] — and it can click, and you go on a heater."
Even compared to heaters of the past, though, this one is unlike most for Hernández. If September ended today, his 1.211 OPS this month would be the highest mark in any month of his career.
Hernández maintains that his confidence never wavered through the rough patch; that he knew, at some point, things would turn. His teammates shared that belief.
This was the same guy, after all, who homered in every playoff series last season.
(Photo by Melina Pizano/Getty Images)
"The clutch gene and everything that he has in him, the reason why we got him and the reason why we’ve been so good with him in the lineup the last couple years, nothing changed this year just because of a bad stretch," Rojas told me. "To be honest with you, I was never concerned about it … I want nobody in a big at-bat more than Teo."
After the big hit last month in Detroit, Hernández returned home, made the swing changes and provided the elusive clutch hit the scuffling Dodgers’ offense had been missing with a walk-off double to salvage a series against the Cardinals.
That hit helped spark an eight-game winning streak for the Dodgers, who started to look like themselves again.
Their ebullient left fielder is looking that way, too.
"I feel really good right now," Hernández said. "I’ve been working really hard for this, and I’m glad and happy that everything is coming together."

The Dodgers took Monday's series opener, 4-1, behind seven shutout innings from Tarik Skubal. Then, they won Tuesday's game, 4-0, behind seven shutout innings from Yoshinobu Yamamoto.

“A team like the Reds right now, where they’re scuffling a little bit, it’s daunting when you see a starter like those guys that we’re running out there.”
Dodgers vs Reds Pitching Matchup on Wednesday
Snell is looking to continue his run of dominance since returning from midseason elbow surgery.
The left-hander has gone 4-0 with a 1.04 ERA across six starts, striking out 46 while allowing zero home runs over 34.2 innings of work.
Snell, who pitched 5.2 innings in his most recent start, is still looking to go deeper into games moving forward. He hasn't pitched more than six innings in any of his six starts.
“I mean the goal, at worst is definitely six for me,” Snell said. “I also know that I can go seven, eight, nine. I know I’m able to do it. So for me not to, I just have to get more efficient early in the game. I feel like once I get past the first couple innings, I start cruising and start figuring it out."

Everyone knew the Los Angeles Dodgers paid more to sign Kyle Tucker than anyone else in MLB was willing to pay.
Even still, it seemed like the deal would be a good one for the back-to-back World Series champs. Tucker has been a multi-tool outfielder for his entire career, and now he'd be joined a stacked lineup that would, if anything, take some pressure off of him.
It sure seemed like a no-brainer for everyone involved.
Somehow, though, it has been a disaster. The Dodgers are still great, of course, but Tucker hasn't contributed to that.
And so in an article earlier this week, ESPN's Bradford Doolittle summarized the disappointing signings of Tucker and closer Edwin Diaz in a single word:
"Ouch."
Yeah, that about sums it up.
Kyle Tucker Stats
Through Sept. 15, Tucker has played 143 games for the Dodgers. You've got to give him credit for showing up every day and trying to break out of a funk that seems never-ending.
For the season, he has batted just .226, though.
Tucker has slugged OK, at least, with 21 doubles, four triples and 15 home runs to give him a .701 OPS.
He also has stolen 11 bases without getting caught.
The problem is that Tucker signed a deal worth $60 million per year, and he's on pace for by far the lowest OPS of his career outside of a 28-game debut stint in 2018.
"The Dodgers' splash signings of Tucker and Edwin Diaz in last season's free agency were the cause of much handwringing about L.A.'s economic dominance," Doolittle writes. "While those high-level, targeted acquisitions looked like no-brainers at the time, the first year of both deals could hardly have gone worse. Together, Tucker and Diaz are at minus-1.0 bWAR for their Dodgers debuts while earning a combined $47 million. Ouch."
Tucker has homered twice in the last five games for the Dodgers, dating back to Sept. 11, so maybe it's a sign that he's heating up at just the right time.
It sure would be ironic if Tucker just coasted through a disappointing season but then stepped up in time to help them win the World Series again.
Edwin Diaz Stats
Diaz has dealt with injuries most of the season and is currently on the 15-day IL, but even when conceptually healthy, he's been rough.
In 16 outings, Diaz has an 11.86 ERA. He's allowed 18 runs (including three homers) in 13.1 innings. Diaz has also walked 10 guys, and while he's struck out 19, the punchouts haven't been enough to overcome the other issues.
At this point, it's not clear whether Diaz can be any kind of help down the stretch and into October.
The Dodgers rolled last postseason with a bullpen that relied on starting pitchers for the most part, and that may have to be the case again.

The Los Angeles Dodgers had yet another dream offseason in 2025-26.
The Dodgers were once again viewed as the winners of the offseason, earning the honor among media and fans for the third straight year after signing closer Edwin Diaz and star outfielder Kyle Tucker.
Diaz and Tucker signed lucrative contracts with the Dodgers; however, neither has panned out anywhere close to where the Dodgers had hoped.
Instead, ESPN's Bradford Doolittle labeled the two as the biggest disappointment for the Dodgers as the regular season winds down.
"The Dodgers' splash signings of Tucker and Edwin Diaz in last season's free agency were the cause of much handwringing about LA's economic dominance," Doolittle wrote.
"While those high-level, targeted acquisitions looked like no-brainers at the time, the first year of both deals could hardly have gone worse. Together, Tucker and Diaz are at minus-1.0 bWAR for their Dodgers debuts while earning a combined $47 million. Ouch."
How Has Edwin Diaz Been for the Dodgers?
Diaz was the first of the two to sign, inking a three-year, $69 million contract with the Dodgers.
The Dodgers made him the highest-paid closer by average annual salary, and as the season winds down, that contract is looking like an utter disaster. In 16 appearances this year, Diaz has posted a 11.85 ERA, 2.56 WHIP and 19 strikeouts in 13.2 innings.
The 32-year-old has blown four saves out of 11 opportunities. On top of that, batters are hitting a staggering .385 against him in Los Angeles.
Diaz has also struggled with injuries. He's missed significant time due to elbow surgery and is currently on the injured list with neck inflammation.
His lack of results, inconsistencies and injuries have cast serious doubt on whether he will even make the Dodgers' postseason roster.
How Has Kyle Tucker Been for the Dodgers?
As for Tucker, he's been available, but just hasn't performed.
The Dodgers signed the 29-year-old to a lucrative deal, carrying the highest present-day average annual value (AAV) in MLB history at $57.1 million per year.
However, Tucker hasn't performed at that level for most of the season.
The overall numbers alone are worrisome. Tucker is batting .226 with 15 home runs, 66 RBIs, 11 stolen bases and 113 hits in 500 at-bats. His OPS is just .701.
Tucker will continue to get everyday opportunities through the end of the regular season and the posteason. If he can play well in October, all will be forgotten from his disappointing first year.

CINCINNATI — Yoshinobu Yamamoto allowed one hit through seven innings as the Los Angeles Dodgers beat the Cincinnati Reds 4-0 on Tuesday night to edge closer to an NL West division title.
The Dodgers reduced the magic number to clinch their 13th division title in the past 14 seasons to two. Los Angeles wrapped up a playoff spot on Monday and still is vying for the top seed in the NL.
Cincinnati is assured of a non-winning season after its 81st loss.
Yamamoto (14-8) made his team-high 27th start and allowed only a third-inning double to Elly De La Cruz, after which he retired 10 straight. He walked two and struck out seven. It was the second straight game a Dodgers starter went seven scoreless after Tarik Skubal on Monday.
Dodgers pitching recorded its 12th shutout of the season. The Reds were blanked for the 17th time.
Freddie Freeman returned to the Dodgers lineup after missing three of the past five games with right knee soreness and had three singles in five at-bats. Freeman was 3 for 30 coming into Tuesday.
Josue De Paula batted leadoff for the first time in just his fifth career game for the Dodgers and went 0 for 5 with a strikeout. He's 2 for 14 since his callup.
Teoscar Hernandez's 15th homer of the season off right-hander Rhett Lowder followed a walk to Kyle Tucker and made the score 3-0 in the third. Lowder (6-11) allowed three earned runs on five hits in five innings.
Alex Freeland made the score 4-0 in the seventh with a solo homer off Pierce Johnson.
De La Cruz extended his on-base streak to 22 games dating to Aug. 22, going 2 for 3 with a double, walk, and stolen base.
Cincinnati had runners on first and third in the ninth against Tanner Scott who struck out the next three batters to seal the Dodgers' ninth straight win over the Reds.
Dodgers LHP Blake Snell (4-1, 1.91) will oppose Reds LHP Andrew Abbott (6-11, 4.84) on Wednesday.

How Teoscar Hernández fixed his swing to help power Dodgers over the Reds
- Click here to listen to this article
-
CINCINNATI — A simple change opened a dramatic offensive turnaround for Dodgers left fielder Teoscar Hernández.
Hernández’s two-run homer Tuesday, in the Dodgers’ 4-0 win against the Reds, was his second home run in as many nights, as the team trimmed its magic number to clinch the division to one behind Yoshinobu Yamamoto’s seven innings of one-hit ball. And, significantly, this one was against a right-handed pitcher.
“It’s been very helpful,” manager Dave Roberts said after the game. “As certain guys are not seeing the ball as well, it’s nice to kind of backfill with guys like Teo swinging the bat. And when you can slug like he can, you can win baseball games, and he can carry us for a while. And the last 10 days, something like that, it’s been really good from him.”
Through the end of August, Hernández had just a .668 OPS against right-handed pitchers this season. So, when Roberts was asked in Detroit whether the Dodgers would consider setting up a left-field platoon with the team’s September call-ups, he said yes.
Hernández homered off Tigers left-hander Framber Valdez on the last day of the series. And before the Dodgers opened a three-game set against the Cardinals at Dodger Stadium, Hernández met with the hitting coaches.
Against Valdez, Hernández was in a closed stance, to delay his front hip from opening, according to Dodgers hitting coach Aaron Bates. But the team’s hitting group thought a return to a familiar setup could be a long-term solution.
“It was a great meeting we had,” Bates said. “We all talked about it, and then he felt comfortable enough to do it, and then the rest is to his credit. He’s just been who he is.”
Edwin Díaz struggled in his rehab start Sunday, and Dave Roberts is making it clear the Dodgers “got to see something” before putting him on the playoff roster.
In the past, Hernández had used a “twister tap” as his stride. He started in a more open stance, tapped his toe in line with the pitcher, and then set his foot down. But lower-body injuries the last couple of years — a left groin strain last season and a left hamstring strain earlier this season — forced him away from it.
His improved health and hip flexibility opened the avenue for him to return to that timing mechanism.
“When Teo’s hips are loose that way, and his front leg looks like an Elvis knee, it’s a good sign for us,” Bates said. “Because that means that he can open and close it without his upper body going with it.”
The advantage of the twister tap, as Hernández explained it, is how repeatable it is. A more traditional stride can be sped up or slowed down.
“Just being able to control my body and being in a good position,” Hernández said earlier this month. “I can see the pitch a little sooner and identify what kind of pitch it is and if it’s going to be a strike or a ball.”
With that change, he’s rewarded the Dodgers for deciding against platooning left field. Hernández entered Tuesday with a .777 OPS against right-handed pitchers — a sample size of just 28 plate appearances but still a significant jump.
“The biggest thing is his plate coverage away,” Bates said. “Because now he can spoil pitches, and he’s staying in at-bats longer.”
Hernández’s dramatic offensive turnaround, along with fellow corner outfielder Kyle Tucker’s improvement, have helped steady a Dodgers offense that’s missing Shohei Ohtani (on the IL with right biceps and left knee injuries) and includes a hobbled Freddie Freeman (right knee soreness).
Rookie Josue De Paula, mostly filling in for Ohtani at designated hitter, has already shown he can take mature at-bats and provide some pop. But he’s still finding his footing in a new league.
It lengthens the Dodgers lineup for Hernández, after a slow start to his year, to return to being a veteran power threat — just in time to, ideally, carry the momentum into the postseason.
On Monday, he launched his two-run shot off left-hander Nick Lodolo. On Tuesday, he replicated the feat off right-hander Rhett Lowder.
On the second pitch of the at-bat, Hernández recognized a hung slider, and he roped it over the left-field fence at 109.3 mph, according to Statcast. The blast put the Dodgers up 3-0 in the third inning, with Dodgers starter Yamamoto settling into a groove on the other side.
Yamamoto had walked the first two batters he faced, but he reined in his control to pitch seven scoreless innings and allow just one more baserunner — a double by Reds star shortstop Elly De La Cruz.
The Dodgers also scored on Hunter Feduccia’s second-inning single and Alex Freeland’s seventh-inning homer. And the Dodgers bullpen completed the shutout.
Freeman staying in the lineup
Freeman was all smiles after his three-hit game Tuesday — after going hitless for his last four games.
“I was supposed to be off tomorrow, but I played myself in there,” he said. “So I’m very excited.”
Roberts explained: “He was joking, saying, ‘If I get three hits, then can I be in there tomorrow?’”
Sure enough, the mechanical adjustments he made in the batting cage — focusing on getting his foot down early and making contact out in front — got him there.
“I’m just trying to find something that gives me results,” Freeman said. “We’re at the time where we’re just trying to get hot for five weeks here. So kind of like I did in the World Series a couple years ago, I did the step-out move. That’s not sustainable over six months. I’m not trying to find something that’s sustainable.”
Though Roberts has been trying to find opportunities to rest Freeman, he saw promising signs Tuesday beyond the results.
“Just my eyes, just watching him move, I feel good about him going tomorrow,” Roberts said.
De Paula, Freeland and third baseman Max Muncy will be out of the lineup Wednesday, Roberts said.

With a spot in the MLB playoff locked up, the Los Angeles Dodgers have one major goal for the rest of September: get healthy.
Sure, there are sub-storylines to follow, from Josue De Paula filling in at DH, which bullpen arms are getting hot at the right time, and Kyle Tucker figuring it out down the stretch, but for the most part, the Dodgers simply want to take the field in October with their best guys all available for Dave Roberts to call upon.
Fortunately, on Tuesday, Roberts provided fans with some positive updates on that very front, noting that Shohei Ohtani and Andy Pages are trending in the right direction, as reported by The Athletic's Fabian Ardaya.

"Some more from Dave Roberts: Shohei Ohtani hit in the cage today. Hope is still for him to return before the end of the regular season," Ardaya wrote. "Andy Pages hit off the machine today. Plan is for him to do Trajekt next. Bullpen game on Thursday."
After breaking his hand in mid-August in a game against the Pittsburgh Pirates, Pages has missed almost a month as he works back from surgery. And as for Ohtani? Well, after missing four games earlier in the month, he returned for one but didn't ultimately look right, landing on the IL to allow him to recover from a series of injuries that have hampered his production down the stretch.
Without Pages and Ohtani, the Dodgers still found a way to manufacture offense, ripping off their longest win streak of the season, but folding that duo back into the fray, especially with De Paula proving he deserves a spot on the bench as a power-hitting pinch hitter, makes LA all the more dangerous down the stretch.

Elly De La Cruz is truly ascending into Tungsten Arm O'Doyle territory of late.
Monday night saw him completely destroy a baseball, one that was conservatively estimated at 457 feet as it buzzed past the power stacks in left-center field in Great American Ball Park en route to exiting the stadium altogether. It was reminiscent of the superblast he hit from the other side of the plate off Los Angeles Dodgers ace Tarik Skubal just a week ago, feats of strength irreplicable by just about any other sole on the planet.
The Cincinnati Reds lost last night, though. Elly's homer was their lone run in a 4-1 loss to those very same Dodgers, a loss that officially eliminated the Reds from any miracle chance at a spot in the postseason. It also sunk them to 10 full games under .500 at 70-80, and this season is rapidly deteriorating into yet another one to forget and chuck onto the scrap-heap of memories of this once proud franchise.
I digress.
Rhett Lowder has a lot to improve upon as he heads into a vital offseason for his overall development. Anything short of a rapid change of form means the Reds need to build in even more redundancy in their starting depth plans for 2027, and there's been precious little in the way of advancement from their former 1st round pick so far in his own disappointing 2026. Kyle Tucker's home run Monday in Cincinnati was his third in his last five games. In that span he's raised his slugging percentage from a season-low .350 on Sept. 8 to .376 entering Tuesday's rematch against the Reds.
September is halfway through, and it's shaping into Tucker's best month of the season. If it seems like he's stopped pressing at the plate, perhaps Tucker let up on himself after getting some needed reassurance in a one-on-one meeting with Los Angeles Dodgers manager Dave Roberts.
“I told him, I’m gonna ride or die with him,” Roberts said (via Jack Harris of the California Post). “That was my young term phrase.”
It's been a rough ride for Tucker in his first season in Los Angeles. The Dodgers signed the four-time All-Star to a four-year, $240 million contract over the winter. Despite being baseball's highest-paid player this season, Tucker hit only one home run in his first 17 games of the season.
Things didn't get much better from there. Among 138 qualified hitters through the end of August, Tucker's .683 OPS ranked 116th.
"I was prepared, the organization was prepared, to give him as much leash as we possibly could to work through some things, and I do think that now we’re starting to see the fruits,” Roberts said. “So I see no other reason why we would pivot from running him out there every day.”
Fans might beg to differ.
At Triple-A Oklahoma City, outfielder James Tibbs III has 29 home runs and 101 RBIs to go with a .417 on-base percentage. Prospect Josue De Paula, who's played right field in the minors, was promoted to take Shohei Ohtani's place on the active roster.
Since his debut, the 21-year-old has reached base in half of his first 14 plate appearances. Sunday, he hit his first career home run. Perhaps Roberts needed to reassure Tucker that De Paula wasn't coming for his job to unlock his production, a curious case of reverse psychology.
It will be hard for the Dodgers to take De Paula out of the lineup if he maintains his current level of production. Roberts said prior to Ohtani's IL stint that the team wasn't considering using him in the outfield.
Tucker, for his part, can reduce the Dodgers' temptation to use Ohtani or De Paula in right field if he continues to hit like a $60 million All-Star.

Los Dodgers se aseguran el pase a los playoffs y aspiran a su tercera Serie Mundial consecutiva
El equipo de Los Ángeles se encuentra actualmente en posición de asegurarse uno de los dos primeros puestos de la Liga Nacional junto a los Milwaukee Brewers, que también tienen garantizada una plaza en la postemporada. En la Liga Americana, los Tampa Bay Rays ya se han clasificado.
Los Dodgers de Los Ángeles, que aspiran a su tercer título consecutivo de la Serie Mundial, aseguraron el lunes su plaza en los playoffs tras imponerse por 4-1 a los Reds de Cincinnati. Con un récord de 91-59 y 12 partidos por disputar en la temporada regular, los Dodgers tienen ahora asegurada, como mínimo, una plaza en la serie de comodines.
Los Dodgers se encuentran actualmente en posición de asegurarse uno de los dos primeros puestos de la Liga Nacional —lo que les da derecho a saltarse la primera ronda y a la ventaja de jugar en casa en la serie divisional— junto con los Milwaukee Brewers, que también tienen asegurada su plaza en la postemporada. En la Liga Americana, los Tampa Bay Rays ya se han clasificado.
Los Dodgers, con su generosa inversión, vencieron a los Yankees de Nueva York en la Serie Mundial de 2024 y se impusieron a los Blue Jays de Toronto el año pasado.
Los fichajes de Skubal y Kyle Tucker convierten a los Dodgers en favoritos aún más claros
Tras incorporar al jardinero Kyle Tucker durante la temporada baja y al lanzador Tarik Skubal —ganador en dos ocasiones del Premio Cy Young— el mes pasado, los Dodgers son los favoritos para completar su triplete.
Podrían convertirse en el primer equipo de la Liga Nacional en ganar la Serie Mundial tres años seguidos y el primero desde los Yankees de 1998 a 2000. Pero llegar a los playoffs por decimocuarta temporada consecutiva no ha sido precisamente un camino de rosas.
Una temporada de altibajos
Tras llegar al parón del All-Star con una ventaja de 11,5 partidos sobre Arizona en la división Oeste de la Liga Nacional —con diferencia, el mayor margen de cualquier líder de división—, los Dodgers sufrieron un bajón de forma. La superestrella polivalente Shohei Ohtani ha estado de baja por lesiones, y no se espera que vuelva a lanzar esta temporada; su rendimiento al bate también ha bajado.
Sin embargo, una racha reciente de ocho victorias consecutivas —la mejor de la temporada— ha restablecido la considerable ventaja de los Dodgers al frente de la División Oeste de la Liga Nacional. Sus rivales más cercanos por uno de los dos primeros puestos son los Atlanta Braves de la División Este de la Liga Nacional.
Kyle Tucker y Teoscar Hernández conectaron sendos jonrones en la cómoda victoria de los Dodgers el lunes por la noche en Cincinnati.

Tarik Skubal threw seven scoreless innings and Teoscar Hernandez hit a two-run homer as the visiting Los Angeles Dodgers beat the Cincinnati Reds 4-1 on Monday night to clinch a playoff spot.
Skubal (10-7) allowed three hits — all singles — while striking out nine and walking one for Los Angeles (91-59), which earned a postseason berth for the 14th straight year and pulled within two games of the Milwaukee Brewers for the National League’s best record. Skubal is 2-0 with a 1.73 ERA in his last four starts.
Nick Lodolo (3-5) threw seven innings of four-run, three-hit ball as he struck out four and walked four in his longest outing of the season. The left-hander’s personal winless stretch extended to eight starts in the loss.
Elly De La Cruz connected for his 27th homer of the year in the ninth inning for the Reds’ only run. Cincinnati (70-80) has dropped six of its last seven and its elimination number dropped to one.
Los Angeles struck first in the second inning as Kyle Tucker belted a solo homer — his 15th of the season and his third in his last five games.
Tucker worked a two-out walk in the fourth and scored on Hernandez’s two-run homer that gave the Dodgers a 3-0 edge.
The Reds threatened in the fifth. Juan Brito singled and JJ Bleday walked with one out, but Skubal struck out Ke’Bryan Hayes and Hector Rodriguez to keep Cincinnati off the board.
After Hernandez walked and stole second in the seventh, Enrique Hernandez lined an RBI single to center to make it 4-0.
Luis Mey tossed a perfect eighth in relief of Lodolo.
Alex Vesia entered for Skubal and threw a clean eighth. In the ninth, Evan Phillips struck out pinch hitter Carlos Jorge before allowing De La Cruz’s 457-foot blast to center. Phillips then retired Sal Stewart and Tyler Stephenson to end the game.

Dodgers might be forced to leave Edwin Díaz off postseason roster
- Click here to listen to this article
-
- Edwin Díaz struggled in his rehab start Sunday, and Dave Roberts is making it clear the Dodgers “got to see something” from the closer to put him on the playoff roster.
- The Dodgers placed reliever Edgardo Henriquez on the 15-day injured list and recalled Bobby Miller and Paul Gervase.
CINCINNATI — Even as the Dodgers clinched a postseason berth with their 4-1 win over the Reds on Monday, bullpen uncertainty loomed.
When they get to the playoffs, who’s going to take the ball in high-leverage situations?
Their options are dwindling. Edgardo Henriquez landed on the 15-day injured list Monday with low back discomfort, ruling him out for the rest of the regular season. Edwin Díaz was so shaky in his rehab assignment Sunday that a spot on the postseason roster isn’t guaranteed.
“We have to go with our best pitchers, as far as performance, talent, all that stuff,” manager Dave Roberts said before the Dodgers opened a four-game series against the Reds. “So my bet is that he will be [on the roster]. But there’s got to be some kind of evidence or something for us to sort of bet on. And so my bet is, yes, but we’ve still got to see something.”
The Dodgers clinch a playoff berth with their 4-1 victory over the Cincinnati Reds, reaching the postseason for a record-tying 14th consecutive year.
Díaz (neck) had the worst outing of his triple-A rehab assignment, surrendering five runs and issuing two walks in two-thirds of an inning. The dud put his return timeline in doubt. His next rehab appearance is scheduled for Wednesday.
“I think the world of him, the baseball card looks great,” Roberts said. “But where we’re at, there’s got to be something for us to be able to hang our hat on. And he knows that. He knows that. He wants to pitch well. So for me, Wednesday, we’ll be watching closely.”
So, who’s still in play?
Tanner Scott remains Roberts’ go-to in save situations. And Alex Vesia, Evan Phillips, Brock Stewart, Jack Dreyer and Blake Treinen all have experience in late innings.
On Monday, starter Tarik Skubal gave the group a much-needed break with seven shutout innings. He limited the Reds to three hits and a walk, cruising through their lineup almost three times in 90 pitches.
The Dodgers pulled ahead by four runs, on home runs from Kyle Tucker and Teoscar Hernández, who have both broken out of slumps, and an RBI single from Kiké Hernández.
With the game still relatively tight, Vesia entered in the bottom of the eighth to face the left-handed heavy bottom of the order. He retired the side.
Phillips and Treinen both were warming in the ninth when the Dodgers got a runner to second base with one out. When they failed to score him, Phillips jogged in to face the top of the order. He surrendered a high-flying solo homer to Elly De La Cruz on a fastball above the zone but avoided further damage.
Before the game, the Dodgers added two fresh arms to the bullpen. They recalled right-handers Bobby Miller and Paul Gervase, as they put Henriquez on the IL and optioned right-hander Emmet Sheehan.
Henriquez will undergo imaging on the area, which Roberts said stretched to his side near his oblique.
“The hope is we’ll get him back in the postseason,” Roberts said.
Roberts said he didn’t know what the move meant for Sheehan, who in his past two starts limited opponents to one run and recorded 15 strikeouts in a combined 11 ⅔ innings.
“Some of it’s probably contingent on Roki [Sasaki], and we’ve got another start coming up down the road here, as far as a bullpen kind of situation,” Roberts said. “So I don’t know, but Emmet’s done everything he can do in his power to force our hand, which I love. The last two have been really good.”
Sasaki (right middle finger blister) could start Thursday. His bullpen session Monday marked the first time he had tested covering the sensitive area on his finger with Dermabond, Roberts said.
“We just can’t put him in a position to go backward,” Roberts said.
The Dodgers also have more bullpen reinforcements coming.
Another bullpen addition is left-hander Kris Bubic, who met the team in Cincinnati and is in place to make his Dodgers debut later this week. Bubic made his last rehab appearance for triple-A Oklahoma City on Sunday, so Roberts said the Dodgers likely won’t activate him off the 60-day injured list until Wednesday at the earliest.
The Dodgers acquired Bubic from the Kansas City Royals at the trade deadline this year. He’d been on the IL since May, first with a low-grade flexor strain in his left forearm, and then a shoulder impingement setback.
In six triple-A rehab appearances over 5⅔ innings, Bubic didn’t yield a run and he limited opponents to two hits and two walks.
Roberts was noncommittal about Bubic being a high-leverage option.
“Seems like all of our games are leverage these days,” he said.
By not putting Shohei Ohtani on the injured list in July or in August, the Dodgers may have compromised the two-way star’s ability to be healthy for the playoffs.

CINCINNATI – On a night when they were nearly blanked for a Major League-leading 17th time, the Reds were once again reminded of what a playoff team looks like across the field in the other dugout.
The only thing standing between the Reds and another goose egg was a monumental home run from Elly De La Cruz with one out in the ninth. The 98 mph fastball from Evan Phillips was actually above the strike zone. De La Cruz crushed it a Statcast-projected 457 feet, the third-longest home run of his career and the longest by a Red this season.
“Maybe I'll pick it up on the way home,” joked Reds manager Terry Francona. “That's pretty impressive. It’d be a lot more fun to talk about if it put us ahead … but it was still impressive.”
The homer, De La Cruz’s 27th, soared into the alley between the bleachers in right-center and the right tall stack as fans looked into the back of the stands to get a glimpse of the ball actually landing. It also extended De La Cruz’s season-long on-base streak to 21 games, the longest active streak in MLB and the second-longest of his career.
But for highlights, that was it for the Reds.
The real frustration of this season was encapsulated by starter Nick Lodolo coming out after six innings, allowing four runs on just three hits. He went over to the ball bag and slammed his right hand into it twice out of anger.
The reason?
Free passes. Lodolo walked four and struck out four while allowing four runs on just three hits in seven innings.
“I think [two of the] walks I had scored,” Lodolo said. “Obviously not every walk you have is going to score every night, but it's something that this year that has killed me. I was just frustrated with it.”
“Oh, I don't care. I don't,” Francona said of Lodolo's reaction. “I care what they do on the mound. I don't care about hitting the ball bag.
“Three hits, but you know, two of them left the ballpark, [and one] after a walk. But still ... it's a dangerous team over there. We got behind the wrong guy.”
Lodolo (3-5) made two mistakes on the night. A 1-0 fastball left up to Kyle Tucker, who crushed it down the right-field line for a 1-0 Dodgers lead in the second. His second mistake -- a first-pitch 91.6 mph fastball that Teoscar Hernández lifted just over the fence in right-center for a two-run roundtripper and a 3-0 Dodgers lead in the fourth, after a walk to Tucker.
That was more than enough for Tarik Skubal (10-7), the big addition that the Dodgers traded for at the Deadline. He blanked the Reds on three hits, striking out nine and walking one in seven innings.
“Obviously, one of the best pitchers in the league, if not the best,” Lodolo said. “So you know that going into the game. But regardless who's on the other side, I'm more worried about doing my job and letting our guys handle that. My job is to keep us in the game, give us a chance to win. ... When a guy's rolling like that, you're trying to match it.”
Before the tape-measure blast from De La Cruz in the ninth, the Reds had one threat all night. In the fifth, they had Juan Brito at third and JJ Bleday at second with two outs. But Skubal fanned Héctor Rodríguez to keep Cincinnati off the scoreboard.
Frustration has been a common theme in the past week, as the Reds have dropped six of their past seven games, including four to the Dodgers.
Ironically, the win by the Dodgers Monday night at Great American Ball Park clinched their 14th straight playoff appearance. In those 14 years, the Reds have qualified for the playoffs just three times, including last year, when the Dodgers started their run to a second straight World Series title with a two-game sweep of the Reds in the NL Wild Card round.

CINCINNATI –– With his already career-worst season reaching nightmarish new depths, Kyle Tucker was pulled aside recently by Dodgers manager Dave Roberts.
The topic of conversation: The $240 million outfielder’s playing time over the rest of the season.
Externally, of course, calls had been mounting for Tucker to be platooned, if not outright benched, as his numbers continued to plummet amid an ongoing second-half slump.
Internally, however, the Dodgers had decided to double down on their faith in this offseason’s marquee free-agent signing.
Thus, the message Roberts delivered was simple.
“I told him, I’m gonna ride or die with him,” Roberts shared this weekend.
In that exact phrasing?
“I did,” Roberts joked. “That was my young term phrase.”
On this day, Roberts had reason to laugh. The previous two games, Tucker had finally offered signs of life at the plate, posting back-to-back performances with three hits and a home run. Over the last week, Dodgers hitting coaches believed they had finally found a breakthrough with the left-handed slugger’s swing, one that (at least temporarily) cleaned up some mechanical flaws that had hampered him all year.
Alas, in Tucker’s 2026 campaign, no turnaround was ever going to be that simple.
Over the two games since, he has gone 0-for-8 again, including a strikeout with the bases loaded in the top of the ninth on Sunday. On the season, his numbers remain unthinkably disappointing, with a batting average of .226, an OPS of .692 and an almost negligible 0.3 mark in wins above replacement.
At this point, it is all adding up to a lost season for the 29-year-old, who is threatening to become one of the biggest free-agent flops in at least the sport’s recent high-priced history.
And yet, the Dodgers aren’t wavering from their commitment to keep playing the four-time All-Star, rolling the dice “talent level” and “proven track record,” as Roberts cited, by keeping him in the lineup for the long haul.
“I was prepared, the organization was prepared, to give him as much leash as we possibly could to work through some things, and I do think that now we’re starting to see the fruits,” Roberts said. “So I see no other reason why we would pivot from running him out there every day.”
The only caveat Roberts offered: “I guess, to that same point, until you can’t, right?”
Trying to identify the root cause of Tucker’s dismal season has been about as easy as discerning his emotions through his stoic and reserved facade.
The one thing everyone has agreed on: “It’s purely mechanical,” as co-hitting coach Robert Van Scoyoc told the California Post recently. “His swing plane is pretty unique, but it’s just not working the way that it used to.”
The problem, as Tucker himself conceded last month, has been finding an answer or adjustment that works.
“I feel like I’ve tried just about everything,” he said. “And every time I feel like I’m turning a corner, I get hit with a roadblock.”
Tucker’s swing has always been atypical, both in the way he “lays the bat back” in his stance (which, according to fellow hitting coach Aaron Bates, leads to a longer path in which “his margin for error is a little smaller”) and how he strides through the ball (launching off his back foot with an almost Scottie Scheffler-esque follow-through).
When it’s all synced up, it makes him one of the most consistent hitters in the game; reminiscent to some evaluators of a modern-day Ted Williams.
But when it’s not…
“I think it’s a slippery slope,” Bates said.
Only now, the Dodgers are hoping they have found a way to potentially end the slide.
For much of the year, Bates said Tucker was struggling to replicate his old, inside-out swing path. Instead, he was “cutting down and across the ball,” preventing him from squaring up heaters or adjusting to off-speed pitches. According to MLB’s Statcast system, his rate of “barreled” balls has fallen almost in half as a result, from 10.8% last year (and 12.9% in 2024) to 6.3% this season.
Their initial attempt at a fix was having Tucker cycle through old drills and mental cues he had used in his career previously. Only this time, those old band-aids failed to make a difference, leaving a player who once always had offensive answers toiling with only growing mechanical questions.
Why that is still confounds the Dodgers. Theories have ranged from a slow adjustment to his new surroundings, to potential lingering side effects from the hand fracture he played through last season with the Chicago Cubs.
“It definitely seems like things kind of shifted after [that],” Van Scoyoc said, noting that Tucker also struggled down the stretch in 2025. “So it could be that, but it might not be. We don’t exactly know.”
What was clear was the need to try something different. Thus, there has been constant trial-and-error in Tucker’s elongated batting-cage sessions of late.
Last week, something finally clicked. As Bates described it, Tucker found comfort with the thought of a “no-roll swing” –– where instead of flipping his hands at the end of his follow-through, he keeps them more square to the big part of the field.
“Guys who throw right-handed but hit lefty, it’s something they struggle with sometimes, because the right side of their body is the dominant side,” Bates said, noting that the team has made similar adjustments with Tommy Edman, Alex Freeland and Dalton Rushing this season.
In Tucker’s case, the cue helped flatten his swing.
“He was missing pitches he thought he needed to get on top of,” Bates said, “and needed to think about swinging high instead of swinging down.” It has also kept his barrel in the zone longer, allowing him to re-adjust to off-speed offerings (one of his great strengths as a hitter for most of his career) while better squaring mistakes left over the plate (like the hanging inside sweeper he belted for a grand slam on Friday).
“There’s a lot more room for error hitting the ball, because you can hit it deep and go the other way or catch it out in front and pull it a little bit more,” Tucker explained. “Just trying to be consistent with that and be as long through the zone as possible.”
Whether it proves to be a genuine breakthrough, or just another false start in a season that’s never gotten going, the Dodgers are willing to keep taking the time to find out.
After all, while Tucker’s regular season is beyond salvaging, Van Scoyoc maintained that “he can find it in one swing and then go on a run.”
Thus, they will “ride or die” with him the rest of the way, despite the dismal struggles the last five months have wrought.
“I mean, the numbers probably are what they are, but we’ve got a lot of important games coming next month,” Tucker said, eyeing what he hopes will be validation in the playoffs. “That’s the most important thing … As long as you win the game and kind of contribute to that in some way, that’s all you can really try and do.”
Added Roberts: “If you perform at the right time, all is forgotten.”
